blocks.x: Okay, let's see. I'm going to put a little something on here first. We're recording today at 905 Edinburgh Street in New Orleans, and today is April, do you know the date,
Mr. Risley? Well, I think it's 6th. No?
April 7th, 1961. And could we get your names on here?
Well, I'm David Dutcher. I'm an attorney from Grand Rapids, Michigan, and I also like to, I like Dixieland music and I play trombone.
And yours, Risley?

My name is William Risley. During my music career, I was better known as Bebe Risley. I lived in 907 Edinburgh Street. I first played bass violin, then I played trombone, and I played drum. And so I lost my health.

Let me put my name on here. I'm Dick Allen. Okay. He wanted to ask you some questions about trombone playing. He just was asking you one, so I thought we'd better get the machine on before you explain too much. Ask him the question again.

The question, Risley, I've had this formal education in playing trombone in concert bands, in marching bands. But I'm always playing set notes of music, something that somebody else has written for me. And I'm very enchanted by this Dixieland music where the trombone player seems to be making it up and improvising and playing things that aren't written. And the music is a very happy type of music, which I think is good for relaxation for lawyers, among other people. And I'm wondering, how do you play, what do you think of when you play this Dixieland music?

Well, at our time back there, you know, we wasn't much of a reader. Spellers, and the trombone, he didn't do much. Most of the time he had bass licks, you know. And then he had nod, then he'd have a little solo or something. But he didn't play trombone like those fellas. The most was a gift, and we done most sliding and faking on such an audible step, you see. We couldn't play no trombone like those boys were playing that they didn't know how. You see, and which was just mostly a gift. And most of us played from ear on trombone. There wasn't many of the, Ory wasn't a reader, Jack Carey wasn't a reader, I was a little bit better reading what they were, but not much. And many of the other trombone, Frankie Dusen didn't read, and Willie Connish didn't read. And most of the trombone, Buddy Johnson, he was a reader, a little bit, but his brother Yank didn't read. Vic Jasper was a reader, you see, and trombone
played. Of course there wasn't much Dixieland music written at that time anyway. Weren't you fellas making it up as you went along, or was there some stuff written? Well, most of

the time, which was made up. And we would get an orchestra, you know, orchestration, and if we could get the melody of it, the lead like that, you see, the rest of us would fake our way through, make our parts. Make your parts. Make our parts like that.

If you wanted, if you had the money and wanted to buy the orchestrated parts, they wouldn't have been available anyway, would they? I mean... We couldn't handle them. We couldn't play them all. Were they even written? I mean, say, the orchestration to the saints, was that

written anywhere, the trombone part? No. No. That's the old Baptist hymn when the saints go marching in. Now that was for church, you know, the hymn. And they're taking it, and just like you see them playing today, there wasn't no dancing or nothing like that kind.
So there wasn't any Dixieland orchestrated music that you could buy if you had the money?

For marching, for a saints go marching in? No. I see. There wasn't nothing like that. Same as a high society. There wasn't a, no orchestration for high society. High society, piku, you know, like the military band was part, marching band. Mm-hmm. Piku, taking the piccolo part, you see, that could have been written by Susie, or some of the other great writers, you see. I see. He taking the piccolo part and rearranged a clarinet part. Now I don't know whether it was high society's name or not, but that's the name we're given. But that's how that come about. I see. Piku got it from a piccolo part, from a band, it was all written, could have been Susie, some of those great writers, you know, but of the piccolo part. But see, the piccolo was great at that. Now he rearranged it, from a piccolo to clarinet part. And then that took the melody line out of that particular piece
and made a new piece out of the melody line. Yeah. And made clarendina everybody,

and he called it high society. High society. And that's how he could play. I see. Him, George Bacchier, and a fellow called Tio, them as the men who played at the same. Which Tio? Which one, though? Oh, yeah, now the clarinet player, Lorenzo Tio. See, all of the Tios, all those old men, you know, they've been there, they're professional clarinet players. Them old men, they've been there, but Tio was the... The younger one. The guy used to be with Tio in the 20s? Yeah, he used to play with me. He was with us all along around that time. In the street, huh? Yeah.
He was with you in what band? Tuxedo. Orchestra or brass band? No, in both.

Both, huh? Both. Now, you see, the orchestra, that was my band. I'm taking care of that, the dancing. And the Millard and Herbert band was Celestand. See, he didn't bother the orchestra and I didn't bother the orchestra. If they'd come to me and want to play an old funeral or something like that, I'd send them to him. I see. And if they wanted a dance or or anything like that, he would send them to me. And that's how we got along. And whatever it was, well, we'd split the difference. But they were the same men playing both things? Same men playing both. I see.
Somebody had to go out there and it all?

The Trimble Hump, we used to slide high, way up, you know, and all kinds of different things like that, you know. So on. Like those fellas do. Yes. Did you flutter tongue too? No, we didn't do that. Like triple tongue, they call it.
A triple and double tongue, you didn't do that?
Double tongue, no. Jack Kerry could do it a little bit. He was the only one at that time.
I was thinking more of this tailgate, what they call a tailgate, kind of a spitting tone that they do.
Did you do that? We could do that, yeah. You go . Oh yeah, we could do that. How would you do that, anyway?
Well, that was in the tongue. Just fluttered the tongue against the back of the teeth? Yeah. Is that the way you did it? I still can't do that. Well, that's easy.
Even I can do that. You can do it.
On a horn, you mean? Yeah. Is that right?
And I haven't played in years.
Is that right?
I used to take from FESH, you remember?
Uh-huh, yeah.
First time I met you, we were talking about FESH.
Yeah. I can't get a sustained tone out of it. I can do it a little bit, but then these fellas, they can do it for two measures. Keep it right on coming. Practice.
That's what it is, practice. I mean, you can get your teeth, tongue between your teeth.
Who was the first one to think of doing, playing that tailgate idea? Well, I think Jack Carey.
He was the first one I heard.
But I mean that flutter thing that we're speaking of. Jerry, that was his idea. Yeah, Jack, yeah. Was he older than you or?
Well about the same. About the same. I don't know, I could have been a little older than him.
I see. It's real popular in today's Dixieland bands that fluttered to me.
They're using it. They're using it very much. I listen to them sometimes when they're little boy cutting them, trombone, just like a trumpet or anything else. You see? Yeah.
We could something.

We never did have a night at the trombone. Someone would be playing like that in dancing music. We'd learn as to bump and bump, bump, like a ba, a solo ba, ba, and so on. Until we used to rip and slide and get all that. But we used to get along. We used to like it.
Well, when you play Dixieland music, the trombone part, you say you're thinking of the bass part.

It's the humming, that's what Raleigh said, it's just the humming bass part. Humming bass part. Yeah, the trombone. See, you didn't cut it like the bass violin, but you could use more of that solo. Then you could make your add to it, too. You see, we used to add a whole lot to it.
Well, what did you think about when you added to it? Did you try to harmonize with the trumpet or did you try to play when the trumpet wasn't playing to fill in the holes?

You could do it either way. You could play along with him. You see, if you'd play along with him, then he would play like a second part on the trumpet or something like that, you see? Right. You'd be holding the lead like that, you see?
You had trombone lead early.
Yeah, how's that?
You had trombone lead early, way back. The trombone would take the lead.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. Would the trombone usually have the lead instead of the trumpet? And the things that we would make, you know, get together. Or you could steal it from the orchestra, you see. You could steal a part like that from the orchestra and make your trombone part. And if you had a corner with good ears, like Lewis Armstrong, you could play a third corner. See? One of the ears, you couldn't lose that boy on the wing.
When you say, when you steal it from the orchestra, what do you mean by that? Well, make your part. You mean make up a new part?
Yeah. Make your part and play it the way you want. Right.

When you had the lead. Yeah. Right. Take the melody, right. Take it the way you want. But in those days, would most of your pieces be, would the melody line be held by the trumpet or by you on the trombone?

No, the most by the trumpet. By the trumpet. We used the cornet at that time, see? Cornet. But the trumpet wasn't famous when I was playing. I see. So I wouldn't know what to tell you, how the trumpet and trombone were together, you see? Right. Well… But I know plenty of times we played a plenty of lead, and I liked the tune we used to play. Marilyn, the giga-cow. That had a fine trombone solo in that, you see? Yeah. Bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum-bum. That's a good trombone solo, you see? Just played. And many others that probably just couldn't recall, you know? We could just sit down and get together and make them, and then the, like records and things like that. Or the band, we would get together, or say like a day like this, and we'd come here, and we'd have our rehearse, probably would be there three or four hours. After something we wanted to learn, and if one fellow would get in, we had a clown at play with Zeb Lonerese. He didn't really know him. No, but I heard plenty about him from Fass.
And he had a very good ear for catching from the records, you see?
Oh, I see. There was no reading clown at play. Uh-huh. Couldn't read. But he could catch.
He had a very good ear, and he could catch that, and then he'd help you make your part,
you see? He'd come back and tell you what would work well with his.
Yeah, yeah.
Work along with him. I see. And we used to clean up on that. How long, if you were starting on a new tune like that, taking it off a record or something,
how long on the average would it take you to work up a piece? A day?
We'd be at it one or two hours and couldn't get it. I see. And we'd bring it up for the next rehearsal, I guess.
But after four or five hours, you generally have it put together?
Yeah, we have it put together.
And when you played that piece as the years went by, would you always play it approximately the same way that you worked it out?

Same. Same way that come off the record. I see. But now you would be, many times, see, we was very good on getting that, as far as it was very good, you see? Uh-huh. And we would get out and play those things before the other fellas would get them, you see? Oh, I see. And you'd make your hits, you see? Because they'd hear them on records, you see, or sit down and listen down and stuff, and they did their dancing. And when it came out, we'd be playing it. Well, then we would be playing it.
I see.

And then, Mutt Carey could sit on the bandstand and the Blackwood playing four hours. He could sit there and think of something, and before we leave there, he would play. You know, just get things together. He'd always come with something and he'd name it, just to give us some more funny name or something like that. And the people used to like it.
You mean he would think up a new tune and write on the bandstand?
Well, I think if he'd just been there, it wouldn't be much, you see.
Oh, I see. It wouldn't be much.

Maybe a repeat of, you see, about eight bars or something like that repeated, and then you'd add something else to it, and some other fella was in there, they'd clear on that there, he'd catch a little show, you see. I see. And everybody think if a trombone player was active, he could see something in there, too, you see.
I see.
And Mutt Carey was very good for that, and Buddy Petit.

Well, let's say that today was the day that we worked out for the first time in Maryland, my Maryland, and then you worked out the parts that you were going to play, and you'd probably play five or six choruses, the band would total, seven or eight choruses, and you had that all worked out. When you started playing it, would you play the same notes pretty much every time in the weeks and the months as they went by? That you worked out that first day in Maryland? That trombone solo? Well, no, not just the solo, but all the back parts and everything that you were playing.

Yeah, you see, outside of that solo, most of the time, someone like used to vamp his way through, you know, like a bass violin, you know, and he'd make him say, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, you know, all those kind of stuff like that. And then if it could go high, you'd sing or something like that, some of that would go low, you know, but most of them that would be this style, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, and then make him.
Would you do that in higher registers too? Yeah, you could do that in higher registers too?
Yeah, you could do that in higher registers. Yeah, it could sound good. Do you try to do it up? I could do it, yeah. Well, I never was a real high one, but I couldn't make B-flat, you see.
That's about my limit.
See, I could sing B-flat, I could sing B-flat then slightly.
That's B-flat above middle C? Yes.
Right. Yeah, middle C, oh yeah. Above middle C. That's B-flat above the staff. Yeah. Not just above the staff, but…
You see, you have B-flat in the staff and you have B-flat above.
I mean B-flat one line above. I mean one space I think it is B-flat. The trombone can't reach the next…
Yeah, then the space above.
Yeah. Where you go up an octave higher than that. Yeah. The trombone… Well, that's high enough you don't want to be fighting the trumpet.

Oh, so, Nora Dutre and Eddie Atkin, they could go above that. They was high, man. They could hit F probably. I don't know what it was hit up there, but they could go higher than that. Nobody ever hits a B-flat above that B-flat. No, not that B-flat. No, no, no. So, it's only one B-flat that we can be talking about. No. This is C. It could be F. That's mostly…
F would be about it.
Yeah, I guess some of those bebop trombone flats can go that high. Yeah, C. Can't. They have funny mouthpieces and everything.
This Dickey Nelson that plays with Scobie today can go that high. They were really…
Noor was really good. He could sing high, very high. Eddie Atkin could sing high. Well, Ory wasn't too high, but he had plenty of stuff with the Chino.

Well, Ridgely, when you played this music, other than…we're talking about Maryland now, except for your solo, when you're playing these bass parts, bum, bum, ba-ba-bum, bum, bum, bum, would you have a set pattern so that every time you played Maryland as the weeks went by, you'd put the bum, bum, ba-ba-bum, bum, bum, bum in the same spot as before, or did you just relax and improvise when you were playing that type of background?
That's what you would do.
You wouldn't play that part the same way every time that you did it? No. No. No. I mean, you would memorize the melodies, but not the… Yeah.
I could make two, three different changes like that on some things, you see. Some and some I couldn't get anything out of it.
Two or three different changes now. Could you explain to me what you mean by that?

Well, I think you were going to play like the original part in Maryland would be like we carry that solo. The which? Carry that trombone solo. Play the melody. Right. And then you could put that in there too, if you know how to get it in. Yeah. Different things like that.
Right.
Or like that. Then other things you could do the same thing. When hard level would just keep on carrying that same hard level.
You would always have variations in other words.
Variations too, actually. Yeah.
When, let's say we're just starting off and you're playing this background music now, old Maryland, my Maryland. As soon as you start playing, do you call it a riff or a…
A lick he said. A lick.
Is that what you would call it? Bum bum, a bum bum bum bum bum bum. Would you call that a lick or what?
Well, I'll tell you, I wouldn't know what to call it, unless you just put it in there. I see.

Well, let's call it a lick so we'll have something to talk about. Yeah. Before you start that lick, do you know what you're going to do ahead of time? Is your mind told you ahead what you're going to do? Yeah, yeah, yeah.
You know you're going to do that.
I see. You never start playing a lick before you know what lick you're going to complete. That's right. So you know where you're going before you start.

Boy, that's the best way always, you see. To know that's the same as going up the ladder down, you know, where you're going to stop when you go, you know where you're going to stop when you come down. Now you just go into, like you said, putting that lick as you call it like that. You have to know that in the band, you have to know it too. And then they expect that out of you.

They expect that from you. Yeah. Well, now if they expect that from you, and you're, say you've got, you're going to play six choruses at Maryland, then don't you do the same thing on the other five choruses when you don't have the melody? Or do you take different licks but in the same hole, so to speak? So they expect a lick from you in a hole, but they don't know exactly what lick you're going to play.

They expect, as you said, they expect it, but they don't know. But you know that you're going to make something that's going to accord with them, don't you know? They're not going to throw you. At least make something that don't sound good in that spot.
That'll sound good in that spot with the melody line.

Yeah. You're worrying about it. You carry that melody, that little solo, as we would call it, or Maryland. Then you take that vamp and you use something like that. Now, you know the rest of your band, they would be making something else too. Probably wouldn't be nobody carrying a melody.
Well, the trumpet is resting while you're doing it, isn't he? Most of the time. And the clarinet would be running up in the air, up and down?

Up and down. Then sometimes work with the, you've got a good banjo player, bass player, piano, like that. You see? But neither your trombone nor the clarinet. At least the trumpet, they declared it. It would be in, after you, on your trombone, could be perfect on that, but you're going to do. See? Then your banjo and bass violin and piano would be going along with you. And then when they come in, it would be something different, all like that.
Oh, I see. Could you sing a couple of different licks besides that one you've already sang for us that you might use? On there? Or in any one that you would have? Any of you?

Well, I'm kind of off on that now. But now I knew at the time, plenty of things that I could do. But you see now, you'd make a, you'd have a side action on anything that your trumpet would be playing. You'd have a trombone.
Well, David can hum a trumpet part for you. Sure. Dave hum a trumpet part for you.

Why don't we stick with Marilyn and see. Yeah, they try a lot of them. I'll sing, I'll just hum the melody, and then see if anyone's come to your mind. You see, now you'd be singing that, we could vamp, as we would call it, make, make, make, bump, bump, you know.

See, high and then like that. Bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, high, and they'd be carrying that melody. That's when their chunga would be carrying. So you could bite them nose and pitch them up high like that and low where he can, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, and so on like that. But you'd be in a chord. In a chord, right. Like I'm going in.
You're right, you've got to be in the chord. Can you put that in originally now as I sing it? So I'm not sure I understand where you'd put it.
I'm good. Bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump. I can't get it now.
But right on those first notes.
I couldn't get any tone with it.
Yeah. Bump, bump, bump, bump, bump.

That's how it would be. You'd make that. But you see you sing that and you could have a trumpet player to play that for you and then you could feel your way, you see. You'd have to feel your way and find that. You a trombone player, you see. You'd be hitting then like the bass violin, you see, but you'd be hitting higher or lower and it sounded real good.
Would you swing an octave each time? Bump, bump, bump, bump, bump. Something like that. Something like that.
It's almost like a tuba bar then, huh?

There's something on the tuba bar, but it'd sound different on the trombone. You see. Yeah. Sound good. You see, you could bite them high notes, but they'd sound good. You'd feel it would sing them up there.

Mm-hmm. They really sound wonderful on a trombone. I never knew what the trombone was doing up there, what he was thinking about, because it sounds so improvised and original. That's the thrilling part of Dixieland music is you don't have the faintest idea what that trombone man is going to do. Isn't he the most important man in a Dixieland band?
Well, I don't know. The people love a trombone, right?
Isn't that the hardest thing to do? Because the trumpet man, all he has to do is take a melody line. Anybody can do that.
But you know those trombone players. Like Franky Dusen, he could make good parts from ones and he couldn't read nothing harder. But he could make good parts.
Mm-hmm.
Plenty of them could. None of them couldn't read harder. Just big gaspings. Couldn't read about a gentleman. But most of us was part of the figure now. You know.

Uh-huh. Would you have, when you were playing at that time originally, would you have a group, say five or ten or twenty, of these things like bum bum bum bum bum bum bum bum bum bum in your mind or in your bag of tricks, so to speak, that you might fill into various holes?
You would have, you would have that all the time. You know, you'd have to have it. Right. Come here. You'd have to have that.
And you would use them at different times, at different pieces?

Yeah. Any time, you could be sitting there. Sometimes you could feel it and you could bring those things in, you know. And it would go good. But you had to have, as you say, that you had to know you could do it and have to have a, in there like that. That you wouldn't make a false. Something like that to spoil everything.
Not to make a false. A false would be a discordant. Discord.
Discord. It wouldn't sound good, you see, because you'd be off your regular parts, you know. Right. You always had to be sure what you were doing. And we had plenty of that stuff in mind.
I see. You had all those in your mind and you knew that they weren't good.

You know, we could get by the piano, you see, and if you'd know the melody, you had the melody in your mind, in the air, you see. But you could get by the piano and pick, you know, to go corner, as I used to do, you see. Hitting the chord at different levels. Yeah, I hum the melody and then I would find a note that correspond on the piano. I see. You see, I try to help you in my choir now sing. And I can't play no piano, but I can take the book and I go around by the church and I get the melody, you see. I can play my own parts, just by one thing and two things like that, you see.

Well as you play these trombone parts then, does your mind always picture that melody and where it is? Why sure. You're thinking of that and you're always working around it or something? Would that describe it? I have to do that, I see. All the time in the piece, you're always thinking where the melody is. That's right. You must be.

It was a, sometimes you know, I don't know, you're just like anything else, you just, it's just off, it looks like you just can't get yourself together. Done the game, you're just to, let's get together and just tear them things open like that. The time they would get out on those wagon advertisements and trucking, we used to do all the time like that. But you had to be a good figure. You had to put in something. Because it wouldn't look for you just to come down and play that tune like it was written or nothing like that. Other people, you'd come along there cutting it up and everybody's cutting it up and tearing your pieces. You had to do it too. So we used to play those wagon advertisements all day and we used to meet on the corner, sometimes two, three bands. And the guys would buy drinks, the fellas liked to drink. We had a battle royale right there. Take turns, the bands would take turns. You'd play your friend and group for you, but you had to be good. You had to think, I used to think sometime how we got all that stuff together.
It was a miracle how you did it. All the fellas down there and they came out so good in it. It's changed the whole world of music, you know, that faking stuff.
Yes it did.

Well, originally coming back to what you think about now, you see the melody line in your mind as you're doing this and you have this set of things that you put into the holes. When the trumpet, if the trumpet's carrying the melody, when the trumpet isn't playing, do you also have another bag of tricks or set of things that you play when the trumpet is playing?
So you stop and let you, you know, stop altogether unless you have your way about it. You make your, you fake your own, you see it. So that's what, that's what helped a whole lot, you see.

But when he's playing the melody, now for example in, Oh Marilyn, my Marilyn, right there he's moving. I hear trombones, even while he's moving, doing those things, coming and a counter coming down for example on a music line, they're doing something in there too. What do you think about when, when he's moving with the tune?

See I used to play it, I could play it low, you see. I used to play that, we call it solo. See I would play it low. So low down to the B flat and the voice line up, you see. Something like that. Play that and they could play it low. And I could play it going down, you know, because nobody knows to make the chord like that. I used to do that pretty regular, make my own part. Besides that solo, then I used to go bam, you see, beep beep, beep beep. And different things like that.
So what would you do on this counter solo, when I'm going bum bum bum bum, or the trumpet, when the trumpet's going bum bum bum bum bum bum bum bum, are you coming bum bum bum bum bum?
Well most of the time the trumpet didn't leave that. The trumpet just had made their bamboo . That trumpet didn't play that melody.

When you took the melody? Yeah, we took the melody from the melody. While he was carrying the melody, is there anything that you tried to do to harmonize with him ever, rather than this counter bass part of the business?
Sure, sure. Make your own chords. Find your own chords. Pardon? Find your own chords, make your own chords. It's so often you do that. I see. And we did that in other...
Did you try to syncopate when you were making those chords?
Yeah, sure. Bum bum syncopate, sure. I was thinking, that was good on trombone, you see.

Yeah. Very good. What were you thinking about? Were you trying to get a third above, or two notes above the trumpet melody line that was moving, or were you trying to harmonize with him? Harmonize with him, you see.
You were trying to get two notes above. Trying to harmonize with him. Mm-hmm.

Which you don't want to hit your notes just as he's hitting his. For example, bum bum bum bum. You don't want to be going... No. You wouldn't want to do that. No, no, no. You play how you see, you can play that high.
I can play that high. I can play that high. I can play from B flat above the stairs, you know, setting his up high. Would you be playing your notes in the same rhythm he's playing? Yeah.
No, I mean you'd be attacking your notes, hitting your notes the same time he hit his ever?
Well, you would. Let's see now. You know, if you'd be a fast enough I'd call myself bebbing and then, well then I'd have to hit between him. Yeah. You see him? Just really.

Yeah. But would you ever hit, you know, right with him in harmony? Would you ever play a part in harmony? Let's say he's taking a break. Would you ever work it out where the trombone and the trumpet played right in close harmony and you'd get it in the notes at the same time or anything?

Well you would. You would. Most of it. You'd have to do that at times, you know. At times you'd play right. At times. You wouldn't be too much of it, you see, if you would play eight bars like that, something like that. And then you'd get off from it. Often you'd have to do that.
So you'd have a harmony half a chorus, a fourth of a chorus, and then you'd get away and break away and play in between them, huh? So you'd have a variety that way, I see.
What I'm thinking of originally, Dick would you sing the melody part to Marilyn by Marilyn, I'll sing this other part. I can't sing. Well you can. What you want, Marilyn?

You see, when we would have those things to do, we would just like to have to have a meeting, or just have to come together. You know, some fellas, if we don't add something to it, like if you'd have something in your mind that you thought would help, I would have something in my mind, but we'd try either, you see. I see.
The leader of the band wouldn't dictate what to do.

I mean… Oh, he couldn't dictate because sometimes you'd have fellas in there on making up those things, improvising, you see, more better than him. But, so before I lead the band, that was his job. Now we had some very good fellas, a fella like Buddy B.T. He had a very good, he had a good talent, a good gift like that. Well, he would always have, even like trombone parts, anything like that.
He'd help you with that? Yeah.
Buddy would help you with that. He'd like Mud Carrot. Them kind that would play their part, and they'd say, you make this.
When they had the melody line, they'd tell the rest of you what they liked, they could hear that you could be doing.

Yeah, you see. I see. Then they'd find a part for each fella, you see, like, a clarinet, you know he's always going to be a, a, a, like that. Well, they'd say, you trombone player, they would take the horn, you see, and they would play their part, and then they would figure a part for you to fit in there with them, you see, and then we would practice that. I see. See? I see. And then you'd do the same thing. That's when you're trying to make up, you know. I knew, right.
I knew.
Right. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
I wanted to ask you about the Jack Carey style so he could get an idea of what Jack Carey played like.

Jack was a good, you know, a good, he had a very good ear. He was speaking about that fast tone and all like that, Jack could do that and he was good, he could pop them notes high up there too and he was a good hummer, that means he called a singer on the trumpet. Well that was most of our style then, you know. The singer is the gliss or the slide? Yeah, like that. Now a tiger egg.
You said one time you did play quadrillo, huh?
Once. I remember once we played quadrillo.
What was that for?

For a club, one of the clubs that had you in the city of New Orleans, which is a colored club, and we wanted quadrillo. And we played for them. But I never didn't know much about playing a quadrillo. That wasn't in my time of playing music, you see. But I have seen them dance quadrillo before that, you see. I've seen them dance quadrillo. Now our tuxedo band, you see, many people want to know how the band got to be named the original tuxedo orchestra. See, we used to call it tuxedo band, well of course there wasn't a problem. We called it tuxedo jazz band. And I had a band headquarters on Howard Avenue between Drive and Barone. We had a pressing shop there. And we used to do a lot of work for the Boy Scouts for everybody in them days, you see. Now the man that made a suggestion for us to call our band the original tuxedo, his name was Mr. Sim Black. He was a master of Boy Scout troop 13, and he thought a whole lot of our band. So he came to a pressing shop one morning. He said, Ridley, I come down and have a little talk with you. He says, I believe that I have something that will do the band good. And he said, I was thinking that you all, I said, now the debutante season is about to open. You see, it falls in the air. And I would suggest that you all get black tuxedo suits, derby hats, you see, white tie, you know, black shoes coming in. He says, and call the band the original tuxedo band. And Mr. Sim Black, master of Boy Scout troop 13, give us the, I made a suggestion for us to name the band, the original tuxedo band. I've heard so many stories about it, and none of them didn't know who named the band. But Mr. Sim Black, master of Boy Scout troop 13. So we used to play for them, them boys, all the time. We even went to Kentwood with them when they was on the vacation in the summertime. They was in Kentwood out in the swamp. And we had an occasion to go to Kentwood to play. And so we notified them that we was coming to Kentwood. And they made it possible to meet us at the train, the morning train, took us out in the swamp. And we spent all day with troop site team out in the swamp. And they treated us well. They fed us and everything. And when time was to come and play our job up in the town, they brought us back up in town. And when we, and they came home from that vacation trip, but we almost played a dance at each one of those boys' houses. They just thought so much of the band and the toilet pops and everything about it. And they just wanted to do a dance at each other. They wanted the band and just wanted to give a dance. And so that helped us a whole lot. Mr. Sim Black, he was a very nice man. He took great, he entered his own band. He got many a jobs. I don't know whether he was living there or whether he was there or not. So there was a great man that had lives and young men and things in this town. All the men there now that was on that trip.
Is Sim Black about your age?
He was about my age, yeah. He could be living, Mr. Black. He could be living.
Well, we might try to find him. He might be alive.
He might be alive. He can't tell him. I said his name is Sim Black. Well we can look him up in the city directory, you know they've got everybody's names.
Yeah, and then you know how to find him too.
So that helped us a whole lot from that. We played all those fraternity dances.
We just didn't have enough.

We could have had the two bands that had done them all. But we were well light-minded people and everybody tried to have us. We could go anywhere, anybody would have us in the house. We were always dressed well and neat. It was all right to get along with the people and they were very nice to us. You know, many times. I'll tell you another. Was it going to play any of those white boys that used to play Smokes After Lace Padden? What's his name? Oh there's so many of them.
From here?
Yeah, the boys from here.
Well Louis Prima used to be talking a lot.

Prima. You see now, he was a boy. He used to be around. I don't care where we played. That boy was there. We used to play Highland Baseball part every Sunday morning. Bank of the League. Prima would be there every Sunday morning. And he could ask questions or he could talk. He made money playing music then. He was a fine boy. And we liked him and we missed him when he wouldn't come around. So I asked from him every now and then, but I guess he'd been gun-dated like all the rest of them. Well, it was mighty good. It gave us a mighty good start. Then I would trip down to Fort Worth, it was so good. Then we played in the largest chair in the world. It had a chair that demonstrated going all over the world. It was large enough to take a whole band, drums and bass, violin.
A chair? Just like that chair over there? No, but it was round.
A round chair? A big big round chair. And they put it up on a big float and the whole band could set it in that chair.
Didn't have a back to it or anything?

No. Well yeah, something like that to keep them falling out. We had a back. That's very good. Things like that. Then when we played in the hour playing on Friday, June of 18, 19 and 24, Gitt's aerial circus used to come here every summer. And Mr. George Gates, the president of that company, told us that we were the first one that played live music in the air, Tuxi the band. Of course there had been piano players and different things like that, records and so on, like you said, but we were the first one to play live music in the air. And that job, Mr. Gates helped us a whole lot that had photography, the right set out of one part. And there were many people out there to see us. We made two flights, which was good. And so after that the room went around at Fort White and things. Well that was our biggest year, getting our band together. And we played Trankina's Restorant after Pierron left out there. We played there in one session about nine months I believe we had a contract out there. And we played most everywhere in Louisiana. The colored band, we played New Orleans Country Club, Southern Yacht Club, Chester and Whisk Club. We played all the carnival dances at the anthem there. And plenty of good things. We played in our band. So the people liked us. We made nice money back in that time too.
Did you know a fellow named Henry Lambert way back?

Yeah, Henry Lambert. He lives out in Jefferson. That's the man played with us when we started our band up there and Professor Humperty was teaching I told you he played a, he was a tuba player, he played on, and then he played bass, violin, and the band up there on trombone. Well that was the old man Lambert, but they got a Lambert up there now, still living in Jefferson Pires, his son. But the old man played with us. He used to play the tuba.
Does his son play music?
I don't think. No. I mean, but Lambert played. Well how did you get his name?
From the year before, when Russell talked to you before. Well I'm listening to it, I want to ask you about him, you know who he played with?

The Lambert? Yeah. He played with me, then after he stopped playing with me, he set up a little band of his own up there when I left, coming to New Orleans. But long before that he used to play in all those military bands, like Fumes and things, old man, Joy Moret and all those people back there. He played with them. But when he got into the string band he played up there with me.
He would play with the Excelsior and the Orwood and the ...
Yeah. Played with all of them.
All those old, little town grass bands.
Yeah. Yeah. What about Frank Welch?
He used to be our teacher, Frank Welch.

After I left off of Jefferson Powers, came to New Orleans, and my friend played cornet with us. In the Washington area, too, with Albert Batiste. He was the first cornet player with us. And his boy Joe played drum. Is Joe still alive? The old man, no, he's been there. I think Joe is the ... the ... the ... the ... the ... the ... the ... the ... the but I don't know whether he played music anymore or not. For that, his father and son, he used to play. But that's ... and he's a fine old musician, too. Old man, wacky work. Joe's going to play with him and his boy Joe played drums.
Is Joe still alive?

The old man, no he's been there. I think Joe is there, but I don't know whether he played music anymore or not. I think he'd give it up. Well that's his father and son used to play. But that's, and he's a fine old musician too. Old man, where I go.
Did he play with other bands that you know of?

He played at other bands before he played with me. And he played with Bill and Terry Brass bands and things. He played with them. He played lots of bands in the city. Lots of jobs. He's a fine old man. And he was the one that connected us with Celestine, Frank Wilson. He was playing cornet and he did more plays. And he knew Celestine and he told us in Civil East band about Celestine. We went to see him and we got him. That's how we got together. Now, Emanuel Perez, is that right? Is it Perez? No. Yeah, he was a cornet player.
Emanuel Perez was a cornet player. Emanuel was a, I never did he ever play cornet.
Emanuel Pazze. Emanuel Pazze. Piano, I never did he ever them play cornet.
Emanuel Menela plays them?
Menela, yeah. No Menela Perez. We had good cornet players. Yeah. Menela.
Menela.
Menela. That's who I want them to speak them. And he was a fine fellow, a fine piano player. For them he didn't do nothin' but teach them them.
Yeah, he's been kind of not feeling too well. A dog bit his hand. I wanted to use him on piano and some things. I wanted to dream up some stuff.
Well, he had the name of Wunson being a good piano player. There, great bad joint. He's a fine boy.
Let's get the other fellas in the Silver Leaf up. Like, whose place did you take when you went in on trombone?
Let me see now. I don't know.
They might not even have told you. That's possible too. Well, who took your place when you left? Do you remember that?

Silver Leaf. Yeah. I don't know who they did get to play trombone after I left them. Silver Leaf after we organized our home. I think the band kind of went to pieces after that. Because Celestine and I both left, you see. I don't think they ever got that band together anymore. But Albert Battista. George Sayles, the manager of his daddy, and a bass violin player by the name of Oscar Alps.
What did George Sayles play? What instruments? Banger, a guitar.
He did play banger? He played guitar. And he played, not violin, what's it called? The viola.
The viola.
Yeah. He was a, him and I was back east. I was a violin player. And him and George Orton, I played together. Viola and violin.
Did he play a four-string banjo ever? Or do you remember?
No, he played guitar.
Guitar.
Yeah.
George Sayles. I just wondered, because some of those guys, you know, had trouble changing and some of them liked the six-string banjo.
I see.
You remember Bud Scott and Johnny Saint-Cyr both played those six string bandages? Six string.
Well all the other played with us played six string. We never did have a first string. Who were they?
Who were some of the men that played six string?
Johnny Saint-Cyr.
Yeah, he played, and who else?
And Louis Kevick. Yeah. And who else played with me a while?
What about John Marrero?
Yeah, he had six string. He was good.
I like the sound of a six string. You know you can get those low notes and go upon and everything.

Well a six string. Full range. I think it sounds, you know, you didn't make it look like pure like that. So then the fellas can't get over a six string bandage would be good but they can get over a four. But they hadn't got the sound like the six.
Let's see if we got the drummer's name with the silver leaf.
At that time? Ernest Rogers. Ernest. He was a good friend of mine.

Yeah, Ernest Rogers. I met him down at Lutzen's with Big I. Louis. He used to have Big Landry. Remember Big Landry on the corner down there? And Benny Turner from across the river. Louis Gallo came in late on the piano. That was fun. I used to love to hear Big I play. He was pretty playing.
What about the 101 Ranch? 101 Ranch?
101, yeah.

We played there for Mr. I think Mr. Albert, what was his name now? We played 101 Ranch a long time. We used to start playing at eight. Playing until wee in the morning when he'd break up. We only got a dollar and a half a night for playing there but we made the tips was good, you see. Oh yeah. That was a rough place but we made good tips in there.
Who was in the band at that time?
John Veen was playing piano. Louis. John Veen?
John Veen.
John Veen. The drummer played piano too?
No, that was his son.

Oh, I see. That was his son. He did too. John Veen playing piano. Celeste on the clarinet. Theo on clarinet. Louis Cantrell on drums. And myself on drumming on. Did you name a bass player? Billy has no bass player. And no banjo? Guitar? Did you name somebody I can't remember? How busy is going to sleep. Look like it ain't. If you getting tired we'll turn this thing off.
All right. I guess you better. Yeah. Okay.
Billy has no bass pedal.
And no banjo? Ghetto? Did you name somebody? I can't remember. How busy's going to sleep? You about to go to sleep.
Look like it ain't.
If you're getting tired, we'll turn this thing off.
Alright, I guess you better.
Yeah, okay. If you're that tired, we'll just let it run off.

segments.title: Recording setup, names and introductions
segments.summary: Allen sets up the recording at Ridgley's New Orleans home and gets the names of Dutcher (a Michigan attorney and amateur trombonist) and Ridgley, who says he played bass violin, trombone and drum.

segments.chapter: Faking parts and the Tuxedo bands
segments.title: Dutcher asks how Dixieland trombone is played; most played by ear
segments.summary: Dutcher asks what a trombonist thinks about when improvising. Ridgley says old trombonists were mostly a gift and played by ear, naming those who could and could not read.

segments.chapter: Faking parts and the Tuxedo bands
segments.title: No written orchestrations; parts were faked
segments.summary: Ridgley explains the band got the melody and the rest faked their parts. There were no orchestrations for tunes like The Saints, a church hymn.

segments.chapter: Faking parts and the Tuxedo bands
segments.title: How High Society was made from a piccolo part
segments.summary: Ridgley says High Society came from a piccolo band part rearranged for clarinet. He credits Picou, George Baquet and a Tio, and names Lorenzo Tio as a clarinetist.

segments.chapter: Faking parts and the Tuxedo bands
segments.title: Tuxedo orchestra and Celestin's brass band with the same men
segments.summary: Ridgley says the orchestra was his and the brass band Celestin's, with the same men playing both. They sent funeral and dance work to each other and split the difference.

segments.title: Slide effects, double tongue and the tailgate flutter
segments.summary: Talk about sliding high, double and triple tonguing, and the tailgate flutter tongue. Ridgley says Jack Carey could double tongue and was the first he heard do the flutter.

segments.title: Trombone as humming bass part and trombone taking the lead
segments.summary: Ridgley describes the trombone as a humming bass part with solo licks, and says the trombone could take the lead early on.

segments.title: Stealing parts from orchestras; cornet carried the melody
segments.summary: Ridgley says players took parts from the orchestra and made them their own. Cornet usually had the melody, and a player with good ears, like Louis Armstrong or Zeb Lonerese, could catch tunes from records.

segments.title: Working up tunes from records at rehearsal
segments.summary: The band took tunes off records, spending a few hours at rehearsal, and played them before rival bands to make hits.

segments.title: Mutt Carey and Buddy Petit inventing tunes on the bandstand
segments.summary: Ridgley recalls Mutt Carey thinking up short tunes on the stand and naming them, and says Buddy Petit was good at this too.

segments.title: Playing the same parts each time; vamping bass licks
segments.summary: Dutcher asks whether parts are the same each time on Maryland. Ridgley describes vamping bass-violin-style figures, sometimes higher.

segments.title: Trombone range and high players
segments.summary: Discussion of how high a trombone can go (B-flat, F). Ridgley says Nora Dutrey and Eddie Atkins could go higher and Ory was not too high.

segments.title: Making two or three variations on a lick
segments.summary: Ridgley says he could make two or three different changes on some tunes, so there were always variations.

segments.title: Knowing your lick ahead of time and fitting the band
segments.summary: Ridgley says a player must know the lick before starting it, and that the band expects something fitting in the gap. Banjo, bass and piano go along while others rest.

segments.title: Trying out licks on Maryland, My Maryland
segments.summary: Dutcher hums the melody and asks Ridgley to demonstrate licks. Ridgley tries vamping high and low and says a trumpet player could help him feel his way.

segments.title: Importance of the trombone and the bag of tricks
segments.summary: Dutcher calls the trombone the hardest part. Ridgley says players like Frankie Dusen made good parts without reading and everyone kept a stock of licks, always staying in the chord and finding the melody on piano.

segments.title: Wagon advertisements and battles between bands
segments.summary: Ridgley recalls advertising wagons where two or three bands met on corners and took turns, and players had to think up things to do.

segments.title: Harmonizing with the trumpet and the counter part
segments.summary: Dutcher and Allen ask what the trombone does when the trumpet has the melody. Ridgley says to make your own chords, harmonize a couple of notes above, and sometimes play in close harmony for a few bars.

segments.title: Ridgley on how much he has forgotten
segments.summary: Ridgley says he has forgotten many things and describes his bass-singing trombone style. He says musicians then knew less theory than today's.

segments.title: How high and low the trombone played
segments.summary: Dutcher asks what share of the notes were above or below F. Ridgley says about half, and he preferred playing higher near the trumpet rather than imitating a bass.

segments.title: Two-beat to four-beat playing, Dave Jones and the riverboat
segments.summary: Ridgley says they played two beats to the bar until Dave Jones, back from up north, persuaded them to use four. He mentions working with Jones on a steamboat and returning from St. Louis for Celestin at Suburban Gardens.

segments.title: Planning licks across the choruses
segments.summary: Ridgley says the whole sixteen bars were thought out ahead, with everyone playing something even during a solo.

segments.title: Chorus order and key changes
segments.summary: Ridgley says everyone knew who took each chorus and varied it per piece. They did not change keys on Maryland but did on The Saints.

segments.title: Maple Leaf Rag and the Red Back Book
segments.summary: Ridgley says Tuxedo played little Maple Leaf Rag, which belonged to earlier players, and that Billy Marrero's Superior band used the Red Back Book. Newer bands change the tune.

segments.title: Which bands the Tuxedo men copied from records
segments.summary: Ridgley says they learned from anyone with a popular record, including Dixieland bands and Paul Whiteman.

segments.title: Hoy Nelli and the band's crowd-pleasing hits
segments.summary: Ridgley recalls Hoy Nelli and Maryland as big hits for the Tuxedo band, with a break and a shout that started as a joke. It stayed a hit until Celestin quit playing.

segments.title: Favorite trombone features and recordings that paid nothing
segments.summary: Ridgley names Down Home Rag and Careless Love as pieces he liked, and says they recorded Hoy Nelli, Careless Love, Tuxedo Stomp and Black Rag but got no money.

segments.title: Banjo players and Sweet Emma's start with Miss Caroline Benjamin
segments.summary: Ridgley praises banjoists Tom Benton and John Marrero, then talks about pianist Sweet Emma and Miss Caroline Benjamin, who helped the band get started with society jobs.

segments.title: White society women playing with the band at the Harmony Club
segments.summary: Allen asks whether society people sat in. Ridgley says young white women played piano and banjo with them at the Harmony Club, but men never sat in.

segments.title: Hugh Evans, the drummer, and playing at D.H. Holmes
segments.summary: Allen asks about Hugh Evans of D.H. Holmes, who used to play drums. Ridgley recalls his father was good to the band, which played at the store.

segments.title: Echoing and answering the trumpet
segments.summary: Ridgley says players answered each other, and that everything was practiced until it harmonized.

segments.title: Whether licks were the same in each chorus every time
segments.summary: Dutcher presses whether the licks fell in the same chorus each time. Ridgley says parts were fixed and played the same way each time, so the band knew what to expect.

segments.title: Improvising or playing set parts
segments.summary: Dutcher says Dixieland seems improvised. Ridgley says it sounded that way but players worked out parts and played them the same year after year.

segments.title: Working out parts with Celestin and other leaders
segments.summary: Ridgley says arrangements came from meetings among the men, as players sometimes improvised better than the leader. Buddy B.T. and Mutt Carey would find a part for each man.

segments.title: Jack Carey's style
segments.summary: Allen asks about Jack Carey. Ridgley says he had a very good ear, could pop high notes and was a good hummer.

segments.title: Playing a quadrille for a club
segments.summary: Ridgley recalls playing a quadrille once for a Black club, though it was before his time.

segments.title: How the band got the name Original Tuxedo from Sim Black
segments.summary: Ridgley tells how Sim Black, master of Boy Scout troop 13, suggested the name and tuxedo outfits, and about playing for the Scouts at Kentwood. Allen suggests tracking Black down.

segments.title: Playing white fraternity dances and Louis Prima
segments.summary: Ridgley says the band was welcome in white homes and at fraternity dances. Louis Prima came to hear them at a ball park every Sunday.

segments.title: Playing in a giant chair and an aerial circus, and other jobs
segments.summary: Ridgley describes playing on a big round chair float and in Gates's aerial circus, which he says was the first live music in the air. He lists country clubs, carnival dances and a restaurant contract.

segments.title: Henry Lambert and the early country bands
segments.summary: Allen asks about Henry Lambert. Ridgley says he played tuba and bass with him in the string band in Jefferson and earlier in military bands.

segments.title: Frank Welch, Albert Batiste and meeting Celestin
segments.summary: Ridgley says Frank Welch was his teacher and Albert Batiste was first cornet. Batiste connected them to Celestin, with whom they got together.

segments.title: Manuel Manetta and Emanuel Perez
segments.summary: Allen and Ridgley sort out Emanuel Perez and Manuel Manetta, whom Ridgley calls a fine piano player and teacher.

segments.title: The Silver Leaf band and who replaced Ridgley
segments.summary: Ridgley does not recall who replaced him on trombone in the Silver Leaf band. It broke up after he and Celestin left.

segments.title: George Sayles and six-string banjo players
segments.summary: Allen and Ridgley discuss George Sayles on guitar and viola, and six-string banjoists such as Johnny St. Cyr, Louis Keppard and John Marrero.

segments.title: Silver Leaf drummer Ernest Rogers
segments.summary: Ridgley names Ernest Rogers as the Silver Leaf drummer and a good friend. Allen recalls meeting him.

segments.title: Playing the 101 Ranch and its personnel
segments.summary: Ridgley recalls the rough 101 Ranch, with one and a half dollars a night plus tips, and names the band: John Vigne on piano, Louis Cottrell on drums, clarinet players.

segments.title: Ending the session
segments.summary: Ridgley seems tired and Allen offers to stop the recording.
